It also leaves rent rules to the state, so a city or county can't set its own limit (83.425). Your current lease runs through July 31, 2026, and the $1,300 starts August 1. Until July 31 your rent stays at $1,050. So this is an offer of a new 12-month lease, and you haven't agreed to it. You can accept it, negotiate, or decline and move out when the lease ends. Staying past July 31 without the landlord's written consent is risky.

Is it a retaliation issue? Only if the offer followed a complaint you made. Before this offer, did you complain to the landlord, the office, or a city or county office about the apartment? If so, tell me what it was and the date.

DETAILS

### Is there a legal limit on the increase?
- The stored text of part II has no section that caps a rent increase. It also has no section that sets a notice period for one. I can't tell you a notice period, because the text doesn't give one.
- Section 83.425 says "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." I can't apply any local rent rule.
- You confirmed that this is a private complex, not tied to any school. Nothing in the facts takes it outside part II.

### What does your lease say about the timing?
- Lease §3: "This lease begins on August 1, 2025 and ends on July 31, 2026." Lease §4 sets rent at "$1,050.00 per month."
- The landlord's offer, which reached you May 15, 2026, starts the new rent on August 1, 2026. The lease has no clause letting the landlord raise rent during the term.
- The lease has no renewal clause. Part II also names no right to renew.

### Can you leave when the lease ends?
- Yes. The lease has no clause requiring notice before you move out at the end of the term. Section 83.575(1) lets a lease require such notice, and yours doesn't. The stored text asks for none.
- Lease §6 does require you to leave the apartment "clean and empty," return all keys, and give a forwarding address in writing.
- If you left before July 31, a different rule applies. Under 83.49(5), you would owe the landlord 7 days' written notice by certified mail or hand delivery, with an address where you can be reached. Rent through July 31 would still be owed.

### Can you stay without signing the new lease?
- Lease §9: "If Tenant stays after July 31, 2026 with Landlord's written consent, the tenancy becomes month to month on the same terms." That would suggest the $1,050 rent, but it needs the landlord's written consent. You could ask for that in writing.
- Without consent, section 83.58 lets the landlord sue for possession and also "recover double the amount of rent due" for the holdover period.
- The landlord still can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)). The landlord also can't lock you out or cut off utilities (83.67).
- If the landlord says nothing or takes rent after July 31, it is not settled whether that counts as permission. One reading is that taking rent is permission, based on 83.56(5)(a). The other reading is that permission must actually be given. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

### Could the increase be retaliation?
- Section 83.64(1) makes it unlawful to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent … primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." You must have acted in good faith. Section 83.64(4) also requires that you be treated differently from other tenants.
- Under 83.64(2), retaliation is raised as a defense "in any action brought against him or her for possession." No eviction case exists here, so there is nothing to raise yet.
- Whether you can act on an increase alone is not settled. One reading is that 83.64 works only as a defense in an eviction case. The other reading is that the increase is unlawful on its own, and 83.55 lets you recover damages when a landlord fails to follow part II.

No. Part II has no section on how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits the amount. Local rules can't fill that gap. The law says these matters are "preempted to the state" (83.425). I haven't applied any local rule.

### Does your lease let the landlord raise the rent?
No. The lease sets rent at "$1,050.00 per month" (Lease §4). Your tenancy continues "from month to month" (§3). Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise the rent. The lease also says it "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (§10). You told me you didn't agree to the increase and haven't paid it.

### Was the letter delivered properly?
It was in writing and handed to you at your door on March 20. Handing over a copy is a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). It also fits the lease, which says notices to you "shall be delivered to the apartment" (Lease §8).

### Is 11 days enough?
This is the part that is not settled. There are three readings.
- **Reading one:** A change in rent needs the same notice as ending a month-to-month tenancy. That is "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The last day to give that notice for an April 1 start was March 1, and that date has passed. Your letter was late for April under this reading. The rent would stay $1,050 for April. Whether a late letter works for the next rent period is also not settled. The date for that period is March 31, which has not passed.
- **Reading two:** No section sets any notice for a rent change. A written, properly delivered letter is enough, and you can pay or leave.
- **Reading three:** Section 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. Under this reading the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy and offer new terms.

Under every reading, the landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy with proper written notice. No reason is required (83.57).

### What are your three choices, and what does each risk?
1. **Pay $1,200.** It is not settled whether paying gives up your objection. One reading is that paying while you know the lease says $1,050 gives up a claim for those months (83.56(5)(a)). It could also suggest you agreed. The other reading is that an increase the lease never allowed isn't rent "due" (83.43(12)). Under that reading you could claim the extra back under 83.55, and each later month would be a new, separate problem.
2. **Pay $1,050 and tell the landlord in writing why.** Quote Lease §§4 and 10. Send it by hand to Suite A or by certified mail (Lease §7), and keep a copy and proof of payment. The risk is that the landlord treats the $1,050 as unpaid rent.
   - The landlord could serve a written 3-day demand for rent. Don't ignore one (83.56(3)).
   - Taking partial rent doesn't stop the landlord from acting on the shortfall (83.56(5)(a)).
   - The landlord still needs a court case to remove you, and a lockout is not allowed (83.59(3), 83.67(2)).
   - If you are sued and raise any defense other than payment, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days (excluding weekends and holidays) after you are served. Otherwise you lose those defenses (83.60(2)).
3. **End the tenancy by written notice.** The deadline for the rent period ending March 31 has passed (March 1). Notice for the period ending April 30 must be given by March 31. It must be written and delivered by hand or mail (83.57(3), 83.56(4)). Separately, if you leave a month-to-month tenancy, 83.49(5) asks for 7 days' written notice before you move out. It must go by certified mail or hand delivery and include an address where you can be reached. Missing that notice doesn't cost you your deposit rights (83.49(5)).

### Could the increase be retaliation?
Only if all of these are true (83.64):
- You did something protected first, such as a code complaint, a complaint to the landlord, or joining a tenant group.
- You acted in good faith.
- You are being treated differently from other tenants. If everyone got the same increase, that points against retaliation.
- The landlord acted primarily to retaliate. A court decides this.

I don't have any facts on these yet. Whether other tenants got the same letter is also worth finding out.

fixed3.answer:
It's not settled whether a letter like yours raises your rent. Florida's landlord-tenant law sets no minimum notice for a rent increase, and it sets no cap on how much rent can go up. Your lease says nothing about raising rent either, and it says it can be changed "only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You haven't agreed or signed anything. You have three choices, and each has a risk: pay the new rent, pay the old rent and explain why in writing, or end your tenancy by written notice.

Before you decide, one fact matters. Before this letter, had you complained to the landlord or a government office about anything, such as repairs or code problems, or joined a tenants' group?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law set a notice period or a limit for rent increases?
No. Part II has no section on how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits the amount. Local rules can't fill that gap, because "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425). If a voucher or other program helps pay your rent, that program's rules may limit an increase. Those rules are outside this tool.

### What does your lease say?
- You are month to month: "continues from month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord." (§3).
- Rent is $1,050.00 a month (§4).
- The lease has no clause that lets the landlord raise the rent.
- "It may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." (§10).
- Written notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address (§7).

### Did the letter work as a rent increase?
The law doesn't say, so there are three readings.
1. **Same notice as ending a tenancy.** A landlord who can end a month-to-month tenancy only on "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)) can change the rent only with that notice. The notice must be in writing and delivered a way 83.56(4) names. Handing you a copy qualifies, because 83.56(4) lists "delivering a true copy thereof." Your letter came on March 20. The last day to give 30 days' notice for a rent period ending March 31 was March 1, which has passed. Under this reading the letter is too late for April.
2. **No set notice.** No section requires any particular notice, so the letter is enough. You could pay the new rent or leave.
3. **Only your agreement changes the rent.** Section 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Under this reading the letter alone changes nothing, and your lease's signed-writing clause (§10) points the same way.

I'm not choosing among these readings.

### What are your three choices, and what does each risk?
1. **Pay $1,200.** Whether this gives up anything is not settled.
   - One reading: if a tenant pays "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Paying could also be read as agreeing to the new rent.
   - The other reading: an increase your lease never allowed isn't rent that is "due" (83.43(12)). Your signed-change clause still stands. You could claim the extra under 83.55, and each later month would be a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)).
2. **Pay $1,050 and tell the landlord in writing why.** Quote lease §§4 and 10. Deliver the letter by hand to the office or by certified mail (lease §7). Keep copies and proof of each payment.
   - The risk is that the landlord treats the shortfall as unpaid rent and sends a written demand. Under 83.56(3), if you don't pay within 3 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays) after that demand, the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement." Don't ignore a demand.
   - Taking your payment doesn't waive the landlord's rights: a landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Whether $1,050 is "partial" rent is the very dispute.
   - The landlord can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)). It also can't block your access to the apartment (83.67(2)).
   - If you are sued and raise any defense other than payment, you must pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion to determine the rent, within 5 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays) after you are served. Otherwise you give up your defenses (83.60(2)).
3. **End the tenancy by written notice.** The 30-day deadline for a tenancy ending March 31 has passed. For the next rent period, ending April 30, the last day to give notice is March 31.
   - Deliver the notice by hand or by certified mail (lease §7; 83.56(4)).
   - Moving out also brings the separate 7-day written notice in 83.49(5). One notice by hand or certified mail, with your forwarding address, in time for both, meets both.
   - Under every reading, the landlord can also end your tenancy with a proper written 30-day notice. The law names no reason the landlord must give (83.57).

### Could this be retaliation?
Only if you did something protected first, such as a code complaint, a complaint to the landlord under 83.56(1), or joining a tenants' group (83.64(1)). Three more things must also be true:
- You acted in good faith.
- You are being treated differently from other tenants (83.64(4)).
- The landlord's main purpose was to retaliate.

A raise that every tenant got points against retaliation. If you don't know what other tenants were charged, that is a fact to find out. Whether an increase alone can be challenged before any court case is not settled. One reading says 83.64(2) makes retaliation only a defense once you are sued. The other says 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, and 83.54 and 83.55 allow a suit.

Part II of the Florida law has no rule on how much notice a rent increase needs, and no cap on how much rent can go up. You have three choices, and each has a risk. You can pay the new rent. You can pay the old $1,050 and tell the landlord in writing why. Or you can end your tenancy by written notice. To end it with an April 30 move-out, your notice has to be delivered by March 31. The date that would have ended it on March 31 has already passed.

Do you want to stay at $1,200, or would you rather move out?

DETAILS

### Does the law set a notice period or a cap for a rent increase?
No. Part II has no section on how much notice a rent increase takes. It has no section limiting how much rent can go up. Local rules can't fill that gap, because the state has taken over this area: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425). I have no local rent rule in the text I work from, so I am not applying one.

### What does your lease say?
- Your lease has no set end date. It is month to month: "continues from month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord." (§3).
- The rent is "$1,050.00 per month" (§4).
- The lease has no clause letting the landlord raise the rent.
- The lease says: "It may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." (§10). You told me you did not agree and did not sign anything.

### Was the letter in time?
The law gives three readings, and I don't choose one.
- **Reading one:** A landlord who can end a month-to-month tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice. That notice is "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). It has to be in writing and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, such as "delivering a true copy thereof". A letter handed to you counts as that. To take effect for the period ending March 31, the letter was due by March 1. That date has passed. Whether a late notice works for the next period is not settled. If it does, the earliest the new rent could start is the period after April 30.
- **Reading two:** No section sets a notice for an increase, so none in particular is needed. Your landlord could say the written letter was enough. Then you can pay the new rent or leave.
- **Reading three:** Section 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. It doesn't let a landlord change the rent alone. Under this reading the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more must end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Your lease's signed-changes clause (§10) also supports this reading.

### What can you do, and what does each choice risk?
1. **Pay the $1,200.** Whether this gives up your objection is not settled. One reading is that paying while you know the lease was not followed gives up a claim over those months. It may also show you agreed. That reading rests on 83.56(5)(a). The other reading is that an increase the lease never allowed is not rent that is "due" (83.43(12)). Your lease's signed-changes clause still stands. You could claim the extra back under 83.55, and each later month counts separately.
2. **Pay the old $1,050 in full and on time, and object in writing.** Say that you don't agree and quote §4 and §10 of your lease. Your lease says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address (§7). Keep a copy of the letter and proof of each payment. The risk is that your landlord treats the $150 as unpaid rent. Your landlord could then deliver a written 3-day demand for the rent or for possession (83.56(3)). Don't ignore a demand like that. Taking your $1,050 does not mean the landlord gave in. A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Whether $1,050 is "partial" rent is the very thing in dispute. Your landlord also can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)). If you are sued, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays) after you are served. If you don't, you lose your defenses other than payment (83.60(2)). Don't stop paying rent altogether.
3. **End the tenancy.** Under 83.57(3) either side can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice. Your landlord can do this too, and the law names no reason it must give. The last day to give notice for an April 30 end is March 31. Under 83.57 the notice has to be delivered by a way in 83.56(4). Your lease also says to deliver it by hand to the office or by certified mail (§7). A separate rule, 83.49(5), also asks for a written 7-day notice before you leave. It must go by certified mail or by hand, and it must include an address where you can be reached. One notice by hand or certified mail, with your address, that arrives in time covers both rules. Which rent applies for April while you are still there is the disputed point above.

### Could this be retaliation?
An increase can be unlawful if it is made "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (83.64(1)). It must also treat you differently from other tenants (83.64(4)). Examples are a code complaint, a tenant group, or a written repair complaint. You haven't told me of anything like that.
